chapter.title_hebrew: הענף הא': סברות החולקים על כתיבת תושבע"פ
chapter.title_english: Branch One: Arguments Regarding the Writing of Oral Law

paragraphs.hebrew_raw: נביא שהיה באותו דור כותב לעצמו זכרון שמועות מרבותיו, וכן כל אחד כותב לעצמו כפי כחו, עד שבא רבי וקבץ כל השמועות, וכל הדינים וכל הביאורים כולם וכו'" וכן ר"ש הנגיד במבוא התלמוד כתב: "כי החכמים הקדמונים כל אחד ואחד העתיק לנפשו מה שלמד, בין דבר שהוא הלכה, בין שאינה הלכה, וכשבא רבי להעתיק הוצרך לכתוב" וכו'. וע"ז תמה הרמ"ז ז"ל דאם הותר לכתוב איך אמרו בתמורה די"ד דברים שבע"פ אי אתה רשאי לאומרם בכתב? וגם איך אמרו "אלה אתה כותב ואי אתה כותב הלכות"? וגם ר"י איך אמר "כותבי הלכתות כשורפי תורה"? וגם מאי ק"ל לתלמודא על רב דימי שהיה רוצה לכתוב הלכה לרב יוסף? ועוד בגטין ד"ס חו"ל להקשות לרבה ור"י דגם בימי הנביאים התירו לכתוב משום עת לעשות לה', ומכל זה ויותר מזה, הניח דברי הר"מ ור"ש הנגיד בצ"ע, ותפס במושלם כדעת רש"י בכמה מקומות ומכללם בב"מ דל"ג בד"ה מדה ואינה מדה שכתב דבימיהם לא היה גמרא בכתב, וגם לא היה ניתן ליכתב, אלא לפי שנתמעטו הלבבות התחילו דורותינו לכותבה" ע"כ. מבואר מדבריו דגם הש"ס שסידר רב אשי, לא שסידרם בכתב אלא בע"פ, ובדורות סמוך לזמן רש"י, התחילו לכתוב, וא"כ כ"ש דס"ל הכי במשניות דרבי, וממ"ש עוד רש"י ד"ה "בימי רבי" גם בד"ה "הדר דרש להו" כתב: "לפי שירא פן ישתכחו המשניות וכו', ואי רבי כתב המשנה לא יתכן לשכוח, אלא ודאי כמ"ש את"ד ז"ל, אמת שהרב חיד"א ז"ל בס' פתח עינים די"ב מהס' תמה על מרן זקני ז"ל באומרו: "איך סבל לומר דעד דורות סמוך לרש"י לא נכתב התלמוד? אחרי כל מה שכתב רב שרירא גאון בתשו' המובאה ביוחסין וכו', וגם מ"ש הרב ר"ש הנגיד שקדם להרי"ף, ושפירש"י הוא כמו שהובא בעין יעקב התחילו דורות אחרונים ולא דורותינו (ובתלמוד ויין עם הגהות הגאון הצ"ח נר"ו כבר עשו מעשה והשמיטו דורותינו וכתבו דורות אחרונים מבלי השאיר זכר לגירסא ראשונה כלל וכלל שרי להו מאריהו דנעשו ההגהות בימים האלה פרצה גדולה, וה' הטוב יכפר בעד) וכאלה דקדוקים שדקדק על הגאון הרמ"ז עיין עליו באורך, והגאון הרמ"ז ז"ל אזר כגבר חלציו בחק"ל יו"ד ח"א בקונט' כונן לחקר דש"י ע"א לברר אמיתות הענין כמו שנראה להדיא מפרש"י דאחר חתי' התלמוד בזמן הגאונים או רבנן סבוראי הותר או לקחו התר זה מעצמם, ולא קודם לכן, "והתחילו דורותנו" שכתב רש"י, ר"ל דורות הסמוכים לו, כמו שהוא האמת שבין התחלת זמן הגאונים, לזמן רש"י, לא היו כי אם ג' או ד' מאות שנה, ותו לא, ונוסחת "דורות אחרונים" הכתוב בעין יעקב היא היא בלי ספק, ושענין זה הוא מערכה מול מערכה בין רש"י וסיעת מרחמוהי, ובין ר"ש גאון ואחוזת מרעהו, שרש"י במקומות הנז"ל, וגם מ"ש בעירובין דס"ב ד"ה "כגון מגילת תענית" כתב: "שלא היתה הלכה כתובה בימיהם אפילו אות אחת חוץ ממגילת תענית, וכ"כ גם כן מוהרשד"ם ח"מ סי' א', וכן כתב הריטב"א שם בעירובין כדברי רש"י ממש, וכן כתב הסמ"ג להדיא בהקדמתו דהתלמוד לא נכתב עד זמן הגאונים, וכ"כ הרז"ה בס' המאור ריש פ' כל כתבי שהתירו דורות אחרונים לכתוב תרגום והלכות איידי דבציר ליבא, ושכיח שר של שכחה, וסמכו על ר"י ור"ל דמעייני בספרא דאגדתא וכו'" מזה מוכח להדיא דרבי במשניות, ור"י בתלמוד ירושלמי, ורב אשי בבבלי, לא התירו לכתוב דאי התירו תפוק ליה מדרבי ור"י ורב אשי? גם המרדכי פ' כל כתבי כתב בשם ר"י דוקא בימיהם שלא היו שוכחין ולא היו כותבין תלמוד וכו', אבל אנן בתראי דכתבינן כל מילי וכו, גם הסמ"ג בלאוין ס"ה, כתב דבימי התנאים והאמוראים לא ניתן ליכתב התלמוד, אבל עכשיו שרבתה השכחה, אנו מתירין לכתוב הכל, וכן נראה מפרש"י בגטין דפ"ה ד"ה תנאי, וכן מהתוס' דחולין דק"י ד"ה דתנן, שכתבו דמשניות אפילו זרעים וטהרות היו שגורות בפיהם וכו', וכן ממ"ש בביצה די"ו, גבי ההוא סמיא דהוה קא מסדר קמי דשמואל, ועיין פירש"י שם, ובקידושין דס"ו וכן ממ"ש בשבת דס"ו דמתני ליה רב חנן לחייא בר רב וכו', ומחוי ליה רב איפוך וכו', ואם היה בכתב איך טעה? ואם היו ב' נוסחאות א"כ הוה ליה למתני שניהם, וכן ממ"ש בסנהדרין ד"פ מתני ליה ר"י וכו', אמ"ל ר"י אבא לא תתני הכי וכו', אלא הכי אתנייה, וריהטא דכולה הך סוגיא מוכיח דהמשניות לא היה להם בכתב כ"א בע"פ, ונשארה סברת המערכה השנית שהיא: ר"ש גאון, ור"ש הנגיד, והרמב"ם, כולה מקשה מכמה סוגיאות ערוכות, ושמועות רחבות, וכבר ידוע דכמה פעמים נדחו דברי הגאונים כשאינם על שורשי הגמרא, את"ד, הגאון הרב מר זקני בקיצור נמרץ עיין בדבריו באורך, והאמת שכל ראיותיו הם כלפיד יבער, אשר

paragraphs.english_raw: A prophet of that generation would record for himself a memorandum of the traditions received from his masters; likewise, every individual would write for himself according to his capacity, until Rabbi [Judah the Prince] arrived and compiled all the traditions, laws, and expositions. Similarly, Rabbenu Shemuel HaNagid wrote in his 'Mevo HaTalmud': 'For the ancient sages, each and every one transcribed for himself that which he had learned, whether it was a matter of Halakhah or non-halakhic tradition; but when Rabbi came to transcribe, it became necessary to write,' and so forth. Upon this, the Remaz [Rabbi Moshe Zacuto], of blessed memory, expressed his astonishment: if it were indeed permitted to write, how could the Sages have stated in 'Temurah' 14b that 'the things pertaining to the Oral Law you are not permitted to state in writing'? Furthermore, how could they say, 'These you may write, but you may not write Halakhot'? And how could Rabbi Yochanan have asserted that 'those who transcribe Halakhot are like those who burn the Torah'? Moreover, why did the Talmud find it difficult to understand the conduct of Rav Dimi, who wished to write a Halakhah for Rav Yosef? Further still, in 'Gittin' 60, they sought to challenge Rabbah and Rav Yosef by suggesting that even in the days of the Prophets, writing was permitted under the principle of 'It is time to act for the Lord [by breaking His Law].' From all this and more, he [the Remaz] left the words of Maimonides and Rabbenu Shemuel HaNagid under further study ('Tzarikh Iyyun'), and instead fully adopted the view of Rashi as expressed in several places, including 'Bava Metzia' 33b (s.v. 'Middah ve-einah middah'), where he wrote that in their days, there was no written Gemara, nor was it permitted to be written; rather, because intellectual capacities had diminished, our generations began to write it. It is evident from his remarks that even the Talmudic corpus arranged by Rav Ashi was not set down in writing but was preserved orally; only in the generations close to the time of Rashi did the act of writing commence. If this is so, it certainly follows that this was the case regarding the Mishnayot of Rabbi. Rashi further wrote (s.v. 'Bi-yemei Rabbi' and s.v. 'Hadar darash lehu'): 'Because he feared lest the Mishnayot be forgotten,' for if Rabbi had indeed written the Mishnah, it would not have been susceptible to being forgotten. This confirms the words of my venerable grandfather, of blessed memory. Admittedly, the Chida, of blessed memory, in his work 'Petach Einayim' (p. 212 of that work), wondered at the words of my venerable grandfather, saying: 'How could he bear to suggest that the Talmud remained unwritten until the generations adjacent to Rashi? This is contradicted by all that Rav Sherira Gaon wrote in his Responsum, as cited in 'Sefer HaYuchasin', as well as the words of Rabbenu Shemuel HaNagid, who preceded the Rif.' He further argued that the correct reading in Rashi is as cited in 'En Yaakov', namely, that 'later generations' began to write, not 'our generations.' (Indeed, in the edition of the Talmud and 'En Yaakov' featuring the glosses of the Gaon the Tzach [Rabbi Zvi Hirsch Chajes], may his light shine, they have already taken action and omitted 'our generations,' substituting it with 'later generations' without leaving any vestige of the original reading at all. May the Master forgive them, for such emendations have in these times become a great breach—may the Good Lord grant atonement.) For these and similar reasons, he [the Chida] questioned the Gaon the Remaz; see his work at length. However, the Gaon the Remaz, of blessed memory, girded his loins in the 'Chikrei Lev' (Yoreh De'ah, Vol. I, in the pamphlet 'Konen le-Cheker Rashi', folio 1a) to clarify the truth of the matter. It appears explicitly from Rashi that after the sealing of the Talmud, during the period of the Geonim or the Savoraim, writing was either permitted or they took this permission upon themselves, but not prior to that time. As for Rashi’s phrase 'our generations,' he intended those generations close to his own, for in truth, between the beginning of the Geonic period and the time of Rashi, there were but three or four hundred years, and no more. The version 'later generations' found in 'En Yaakov' is undoubtedly the same in meaning. This matter constitutes a direct confrontation between the school of Rashi and his associates on one side, and Rav Sherira Gaon and his circle on the other. For Rashi, in the aforementioned places and in 'Eruvin' 62b (s.v. 'Kegon Megillat Ta'anit'), wrote: 'For no Halakhah was written in their days, not even a single letter, except for 'Megillat Ta'anit'.' So too wrote the Maharashdam (Choshen Mishpat, signon 1), and the Rittba in 'Eruvin' wrote precisely according to the words of Rashi. The 'Sefer Mitzvot Gadol' likewise explicitly stated in his introduction that the Talmud was not written until the time of the Geonim. Similarly, Rabbenu Zerachiah HaLevi wrote in 'Sefer HaMaor' (at the beginning of the chapter 'Kol Kitvei') that later generations permitted the writing of Targum and Halakhot because 'intellects are diminished' and the 'Angel of Forgetfulness' is prevalent; they relied upon Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish, who would consult volumes of Aggadah. From this it is explicitly proven that Rabbi regarding the Mishnayot, Rabbi Yochanan regarding the Talmud Yerushalmi, and Rav Ashi regarding the Talmud Bavli, did not permit writing. For if they had permitted it, let the matter be derived from Rabbi, Rabbi Yochanan, or Rav Ashi themselves. Furthermore, the Mordekhai (chapter 'Kol Kitvei') wrote in the name of the Ri: 'Specifically in their days, when they did not forget, they would not write the Talmud; but we, the latter ones who write everything,' and so forth. 'De-tannan'), who wrote that the Mishnayot, even the orders of 'Zera'im' and 'Toharot', were fluent in their mouths. It is well known that many times the words of the Geonim are set aside when they do not align with the foundations of the Gemara. paragraphs.english_html: A prophet of that generation would record for himself a memorandum of the traditions received from his masters; likewise, every individual would write for himself according to his capacity, until Rabbi [Judah the Prince] arrived and compiled all the traditions, laws, and expositions. Similarly, Rabbenu Shemuel HaNagid wrote in his 'Mevo HaTalmud': 'For the ancient sages, each and every one transcribed for himself that which he had learned, whether it was a matter of Halakhah or non-halakhic tradition; but when Rabbi came to transcribe, it became necessary to write,' and so forth. Upon this, the Remaz [Rabbi Moshe Zacuto], of blessed memory, expressed his astonishment: if it were indeed permitted to write, how could the Sages have stated in 'Temurah' 14b that 'the things pertaining to the Oral Law you are not permitted to state in writing'? Furthermore, how could they say, 'These you may write, but you may not write Halakhot'? And how could Rabbi Yochanan have asserted that 'those who transcribe Halakhot are like those who burn the Torah'? Moreover, why did the Talmud find it difficult to understand the conduct of Rav Dimi, who wished to write a Halakhah for Rav Yosef? Further still, in 'Gittin' 60, they sought to challenge Rabbah and Rav Yosef by suggesting that even in the days of the Prophets, writing was permitted under the principle of 'It is time to act for the Lord [by breaking His Law].' From all this and more, he [the Remaz] left the words of Maimonides and Rabbenu Shemuel HaNagid under further study ('Tzarikh Iyyun'), and instead fully adopted the view of Rashi as expressed in several places, including 'Bava Metzia' 33b (s.v. 'Middah ve-einah middah'), where he wrote that in their days, there was no written Gemara, nor was it permitted to be written; rather, because intellectual capacities had diminished, our generations began to write it. It is evident from his remarks that even the Talmudic corpus arranged by Rav Ashi was not set down in writing but was preserved orally; only in the generations close to the time of Rashi did the act of writing commence. If this is so, it certainly follows that this was the case regarding the Mishnayot of Rabbi. Rashi further wrote (s.v. 'Bi-yemei Rabbi' and s.v. 'Hadar darash lehu'): 'Because he feared lest the Mishnayot be forgotten,' for if Rabbi had indeed written the Mishnah, it would not have been susceptible to being forgotten. This confirms the words of my venerable grandfather, of blessed memory. Admittedly, the Chida, of blessed memory, in his work 'Petach Einayim' (p. 212 of that work), wondered at the words of my venerable grandfather, saying: 'How could he bear to suggest that the Talmud remained unwritten until the generations adjacent to Rashi? This is contradicted by all that Rav Sherira Gaon wrote in his Responsum, as cited in 'Sefer HaYuchasin', as well as the words of Rabbenu Shemuel HaNagid, who preceded the Rif.' He further argued that the correct reading in Rashi is as cited in 'En Yaakov', namely, that 'later generations' began to write, not 'our generations.' (Indeed, in the edition of the Talmud and 'En Yaakov' featuring the glosses of the Gaon the Tzach [Rabbi Zvi Hirsch Chajes], may his light shine, they have already taken action and omitted 'our generations,' substituting it with 'later generations' without leaving any vestige of the original reading at all. May the Master forgive them, for such emendations have in these times become a great breach—may the Good Lord grant atonement.) For these and similar reasons, he [the Chida] questioned the Gaon the Remaz; see his work at length. However, the Gaon the Remaz, of blessed memory, girded his loins in the 'Chikrei Lev' (Yoreh De'ah, Vol. I, in the pamphlet 'Konen le-Cheker Rashi', folio 1a) to clarify the truth of the matter. It appears explicitly from Rashi that after the sealing of the Talmud, during the period of the Geonim or the Savoraim, writing was either permitted or they took this permission upon themselves, but not prior to that time. As for Rashi’s phrase 'our generations,' he intended those generations close to his own, for in truth, between the beginning of the Geonic period and the time of Rashi, there were but three or four hundred years, and no more. The version 'later generations' found in 'En Yaakov' is undoubtedly the same in meaning. This matter constitutes a direct confrontation between the school of Rashi and his associates on one side, and Rav Sherira Gaon and his circle on the other.
